claim: Vemurafenib and dabrafenib selectively inhibit the v-Raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B1 (BRAF) kinase, resulting in high response rates and increased survival in melanoma.
source: Vemurafenib and dabrafenib selectively inhibit the v-Raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B1 (BRAF) kinase, resulting in high response rates and increased survival in melanoma.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BRAF inhibitors and their clinical effects in melanoma treatment.

claim: Approximately 22% of individuals treated with vemurafenib develop cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) during therapy.
source: Approximately 22% of individuals treated with vemurafenib develop cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) during therapy.
evidence: This is a cited clinical observation about the incidence of cSCC in vemurafenib-treated patients.

claim: The prevailing explanation for cSCC development during vemurafenib therapy is drug-induced paradoxical ERK activation, resulting in hyperproliferation.
source: The prevailing explanation for this is drug-induced paradoxical ERK activation, resulting in hyperproliferation.
evidence: This statement references the existing mechanistic understanding in the field.

claim: Vemurafenib/PLX4720 suppresses apoptosis through the inhibition of multiple off-target kinases upstream of c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), principally ZAK.
source: Here we show an unexpected and novel effect of vemurafenib/PLX4720 in suppressing apoptosis through the inhibition of multiple off-target kinases upstream of c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), principally ZAK.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches including kinase assays, knockdown experiments, and gatekeeper mutant studies.

claim: JNK signaling is suppressed in cSCC of vemurafenib-treated patients.
source: JNK signaling is suppressed in multiple contexts, including in cSCC of vemurafenib-treated patients, as well as in mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing reduced phospho-JNK in vemurafenib-treated patient samples.

claim: JNK signaling is suppressed in mice treated with PLX4720.
source: JNK signaling is suppressed in multiple contexts, including in cSCC of vemurafenib-treated patients, as well as in mice.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from mouse epidermis showing reduced phospho-JNK after PLX4720 treatment.

claim: Expression of a mutant ZAK that cannot be inhibited reverses the suppression of JNK activation and apoptosis.
source: Expression of a mutant ZAK that cannot be inhibited reverses the suppression of JNK activation and apoptosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with the ZAK T82Q gatekeeper mutant showing restoration of JNK activation and apoptosis in the presence of PLX4720.

claim: Suppression of JNK-dependent apoptosis is a significant, independent mechanism that cooperates with paradoxical ERK activation to induce cSCC.
source: Our results implicate suppression of JNK-dependent apoptosis as a significant, independent mechanism that cooperates with paradoxical ERK activation to induce cSCC, suggesting broad implications for understanding toxicities associated with BRAF inhibitors and for their use in combination therapies.
evidence: This conclusion is based on soft agar assays with Craf-deficient MEFs and triple knockdown cells showing independent contributions of both mechanisms.

claim: Cells treated with 1 kJ/m2 of UVB undergo apoptosis within 24 hr.
source: Cells treated with 1 kJ/m2 of UVB (FS40 lamp) undergo apoptosis within 24 hr (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis showing Annexin V+ TMRE-low cells in multiple cell lines.

claim: UV-induced apoptosis was suppressed by at least 70% in cells concomitantly treated with 1 μM PLX4720.
source: Surprisingly, this apoptosis was suppressed by at least 70% in cells concomitantly treated with 1 μM PLX4720 (Figure 1A–D) compared to control DMSO-treated cells as measured by FACS for Annexin V+; TMRE (tetramethylrhodamine)-low cells (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is quantified by FACS analysis across multiple cell lines (SRB1, SRB12, COLO16, HaCaT).

claim: The cSCC and HaCaT cell lines tested have no oncogenic RAS or BRAF mutations.
source: Importantly, these cells have no oncogenic RAS or BRAF mutations (Table 1), and PLX4720 conferred no significant proliferative advantage to the tested cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) even when used at concentrations that inhibit the proliferation of BRAFV600E melanoma cell lines (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sequenom mutation screening and Sanger sequencing showing wild-type status for BRAF and RAS genes.

claim: PLX4720 conferred no significant proliferative advantage to the tested cSCC and HaCaT cells.
source: Importantly, these cells have no oncogenic RAS or BRAF mutations (Table 1), and PLX4720 conferred no significant proliferative advantage to the tested cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) even when used at concentrations that inhibit the proliferation of BRAFV600E melanoma cell lines (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown by serial passaging and cell counting experiments over 28 days.

claim: Phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 were strongly induced following UV irradiation and significantly suppressed by PLX4720 in cSCC and HaCaT cell lines.
source: Western blots probed for the MAP kinases demonstrated strong phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 induction following irradiation and significant suppression by PLX4720.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis at 24 hr post-irradiation.

claim: Phospho-ERK was slightly induced following irradiation, and at 24 hr, paradoxical hyperactivation in the presence of PLX4720 was observed, particularly in SRB1 and HaCaT cells.
source: Phospho-ERK was slightly induced following irradiation, and at 24 hr, paradoxical hyperactivation in the presence of PLX4720 was observed, particularly in SRB1 and HaCaT cells.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis of phospho-ERK levels.

claim: BIM was not upregulated in BRAF-wild-type cells treated with PLX4720, consistent with intact ERK signaling.
source: Western blots showed that BIM was not upregulated in these BRAF-wild-type cells, consistent with intact ERK signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing no change in BIM expression.

claim: MCL1 was downregulated by irradiation and not modulated by PLX4720.
source: MCL1 was downregulated by irradiation and not modulated by PLX4720, whereas NOXA expression was strongly induced in irradiated cells and suppressed by PLX4720.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis of MCL1 protein levels.

claim: NOXA expression was strongly induced in irradiated cells and suppressed by PLX4720.
source: MCL1 was downregulated by irradiation and not modulated by PLX4720, whereas NOXA expression was strongly induced in irradiated cells and suppressed by PLX4720.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing NOXA induction after UV and suppression with PLX4720.

claim: PLX4720 suppresses UV-mediated induction of phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 in BRAFV600E melanoma cell lines A375 and WM35 at 24 hr.
source: Western blots of BRAFV600E melanoma cell lines, A375 and WM35, demonstrated suppression of UV-mediated induction of phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 by PLX4720 at 24 hr.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis of phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 in melanoma cells.

claim: Phospho-ERK is shut down in PLX4720-treated BRAFV600E melanoma cells.
source: As expected, phospho-ERK is shut down in PLX4720-treated cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing loss of phospho-ERK in A375 and WM35 cells treated with PLX4720.

claim: UV-induced apoptosis was significantly suppressed (approximately 70%) by vemurafenib in normal human epidermal keratinocytes (NHEKs).
source: UV-induced apoptosis was significantly suppressed (approximately 70%) by vemurafenib in these cells (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is quantified by FACS analysis for Annexin V+ TMRE-low cells in primary keratinocytes.

claim: UV-induced upregulation of phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 was suppressed by vemurafenib most significantly at 6 and 24 hr in NHEKs.
source: and the UV-induced upregulation of phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 was likewise suppressed most significantly at 6 and 24 hr (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot time course analysis in NHEKs.

claim: Activation of ERK was observed following exposure to vemurafenib in NHEKs.
source: As in the cSCC and HaCaT cell lines, activation of ERK was observed following exposure to vemurafenib (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing increased phospho-ERK in vemurafenib-treated NHEKs.

claim: The presence of cleaved caspase-3 correlated with high levels of apoptosis in UV-treated cells and its absence with rescue by vemurafenib at 24 hr post-irradiation.
source: The presence of cleaved caspase-3 correlated with high levels of apoptosis in the UV-treated cells and its absence with rescue by vemurafenib at 24 hr post-irradiation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis of cleaved caspase-3 levels in NHEKs.

claim: BIM and MCL1 were unaffected by vemurafenib in NHEKs.
source: BIM and MCL1 were unaffected by vemurafenib but NOXA induction at 24 hr post-UV irradiation was diminished by vemurafenib (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing no change in BIM or MCL1 expression with vemurafenib treatment.

claim: NOXA induction at 24 hr post-UV irradiation was diminished by vemurafenib in NHEKs.
source: BIM and MCL1 were unaffected by vemurafenib but NOXA induction at 24 hr post-UV irradiation was diminished by vemurafenib (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis of NOXA protein levels.

claim: p53 is stabilized by 24 hr post-UV irradiation in NHEKs and this is unaffected by vemurafenib.
source: In NHEKs, p53 is stabilized by 24 hr post-UV irradiation and this is unaffected by vemurafenib (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing p53 protein levels in NHEKs.

claim: The inhibition of NOXA expression by PLX4720 and vemurafenib likely reflects p53-independent regulation of NOXA.
source: However, since BCL2 family members can be modulated by JNK (Tournier et al., 2000; Haeusgen et al., 2011) and p53 (Oda et al., 2000) in apoptosis, the inhibition of NOXA expression by PLX4720 and vemurafenib (Figures 1G and 2C) likely reflects p53-independent regulation of NOXA given that p53 is mutant in HaCaT (Lehman et al., 1993) cells, p53 is undetectable in SRB12 cells, and p53 levels do not change with radiation in SRB1, COLO16, or HaCaT cells, (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NOXA is suppressed in cells with mutant or absent p53, and from cited literature on BCL2 family regulation.

claim: Vemurafenib and PLX4720 suppress UV-induced apoptosis by inhibiting JNK signaling and NOXA induction in BRAF and RAS WT cells.
source: We conclude from our results that vemurafenib and PLX4720 suppress UV-induced apoptosis by inhibiting JNK signaling and NOXA induction in BRAF and RAS WT cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing JNK suppression and NOXA suppression in wild-type cells.

claim: MEK inhibitor AZD6244 effectively abrogated ERK phosphorylation and activation in SRB1 and NHEK cells.
source: While MEKi effectively abrogated ERK phosphorylation and activation (Figure 2D,E), this left PLX4720-mediated suppression of UV-induced JNK activation (Figure 2D,E) and apoptosis (Figure 2F,G) unaffected in both SRB1 and NHEK cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing loss of phospho-ERK with MEK inhibitor treatment.

claim: MEK inhibition left PLX4720-mediated suppression of UV-induced JNK activation unaffected in SRB1 and NHEK cells.
source: While MEKi effectively abrogated ERK phosphorylation and activation (Figure 2D,E), this left PLX4720-mediated suppression of UV-induced JNK activation (Figure 2D,E) and apoptosis (Figure 2F,G) unaffected in both SRB1 and NHEK cells.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot demonstrating that JNK suppression by PLX4720 persists even when ERK is inhibited by MEKi.

claim: MEK inhibition left PLX4720-mediated suppression of apoptosis unaffected in SRB1 and NHEK cells.
source: While MEKi effectively abrogated ERK phosphorylation and activation (Figure 2D,E), this left PLX4720-mediated suppression of UV-induced JNK activation (Figure 2D,E) and apoptosis (Figure 2F,G) unaffected in both SRB1 and NHEK cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis showing that apoptosis suppression by PLX4720 is maintained in the presence of MEK inhibitor.

claim: The phosphorylation of both MKK4 and MKK7 was significantly upregulated in control UV-irradiated cells and inhibited by PLX4720 in all cSCC cell lines, HaCaT, and NHEK cells.
source: The phosphorylation of both MKK4 and MKK7, corresponding to their activation, was significantly upregulated in control UV-irradiated cells and inhibited by PLX4720 in all cSCC cell lines, HaCaT, and NHEK cells (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing phospho-MKK4 and phospho-MKK7 levels.

claim: ZAK and MKK4 have high binding affinities comparable to that of BRAF for both PLX4720 and vemurafenib (estimated Kd below 50 nM).
source: We confirmed that ZAK and MKK4 (MAP2K4) have high binding affinities comparable to that of the intended target, BRAF (estimated Kd below 50 nM) for both PLX4720 (Davis et al., 2011) and vemurafenib, and confirmed activity against MAP4K5 (Bollag et al., 2010) (Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative competitive binding assays showing tight binding of PLX4720 and vemurafenib to ZAK and MKK4.

claim: In vitro kinase assays revealed biochemical IC50s of 187 ± 5 nM for ZAK, 460 ± 41 nM for MKK4, and 354 ± 26 nM for MAP4K5 with vemurafenib.
source: To demonstrate an effect on activity, in vitro kinase assays were performed (Figure 3A–C) and revealed biochemical IC50s of 187 ± 5 nM, 460 ± 41 nM, and 354 ± 26 nM for ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays measuring inhibition of kinase activity.

claim: At 1 μM vemurafenib, the residual activity of ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5 kinases was 18.9 ± 0.5%, 29.6 ± 1.1%, and 25.7 ± 0.6%, respectively.
source: Importantly, at 1 μM vemurafenib used in our experiments, the residual activity of ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5 kinases, was 18.9 ± 0.5%, 29.6 ± 1.1%, and 25.7 ± 0.6%, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the in vitro kinase assay data showing substantial inhibition at the concentration used in cell experiments.

claim: HaCaT cells with knockdown of ZAK showed 70% suppression of UV-induced apoptosis relative to that achieved by PLX4720 in control cells.
source: HaCaT cells with knockdown of ZAK ('shZAK2') showed a strong suppression of ZAK protein expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and of UV-induced apoptosis, showing 70% suppression of apoptosis relative to that achieved by PLX4720 in control ('SCR') cells (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis comparing apoptosis in ZAK knockdown cells versus PLX4720-treated control cells.

claim: Triple knockdown cells with combined shRNA knockdown of ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5 showed comparable suppression of apoptosis to that of drug-treated control cells.
source: Triple knockdown cells ('TKD') with combined shRNA knockdown of ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5 kinases, as confirmed by Western (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), showed comparable suppression of apoptosis to that of drug-treated control cells (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and substantial suppression of phospho-MKK4/MKK7 induction (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS analysis and Western blot showing that triple knockdown mimics the effect of PLX4720.

claim: Knockdown of ZAK alone was able to account for 91.3% of the suppression of UV-induced apoptosis in SRB1 cells.
source: Knockdown of ZAK alone was able to account for 91.3% of the suppression of UV-induced apoptosis in a distinct cell line, SRB1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B), with corresponding suppression of phospho-JNK induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is quantified by FACS analysis comparing ZAK knockdown to PLX4720 treatment in SRB1 cells.

claim: ZAK has been shown to be critically important for JNK activation upstream of MKK4 and MKK7.
source: Consistent with our findings, ZAK has been shown to be critically important for JNK activation upstream of MKK4 and MKK7 (Wang et al., 2005) and doxorubicin-induced apoptosis (Sauter et al., 2010; Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on ZAK function.

claim: Drug-treated ZAK (T82Q)-expressing cells underwent 2.13-fold more apoptosis than drug-treated ZAK (WT) cells.
source: Whereas ZAK (WT) cells were sensitive to PLX4720-mediated suppression of apoptosis (Figures 1D and 3G), drug-treated ZAK (T82Q)-expressing cells underwent 2.13-fold more apoptosis than drug-treated ZAK (WT) cells (bar 4 vs 8; p=0.005), corresponding to 76.9% of the levels of apoptosis in untreated cells (bars 3, 7 vs 8; p=0.08) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is quantified by FACS analysis comparing apoptosis in cells expressing wild-type versus gatekeeper mutant ZAK.

claim: PLX4720-treated ZAK (T82Q)-expressing cells retain higher activation of JNK across 1–6 hr as compared to PLX4720-treated ZAK (WT) cells.
source: Sustained activation of JNK is necessary for apoptosis (Tobiume et al., 2001; Kamata et al., 2005; Ventura et al., 2006), and our results show that PLX4720-treated ZAK (T82Q)-expressing cells retain higher activation across 1–6 hr as compared to PLX4720-treated ZAK (WT) cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing sustained phospho-JNK in gatekeeper mutant cells even with drug treatment.

claim: Sporadic cSCC arising in patients never treated with vemurafenib contained substantially greater expression of phospho-JNK (p=0.013) as compared to lesions arising in vemurafenib-treated patients.
source: Sporadic cSCC arising in patients never treated with vemurafenib (n = 15) contained substantially greater expression of phospho-JNK (p=0.013; Figure 4A,E) and cleaved caspase-3 (p=0.042; Figure 4C,E) as compared to lesions arising in vemurafenib-treated patients (n = 16; Figure 4B,D,E).
evidence: This is quantified by immunohistochemistry analysis of patient tumor samples.

claim: Sporadic cSCC arising in patients never treated with vemurafenib contained substantially greater expression of cleaved caspase-3 (p=0.042) as compared to lesions arising in vemurafenib-treated patients.
source: Sporadic cSCC arising in patients never treated with vemurafenib (n = 15) contained substantially greater expression of phospho-JNK (p=0.013; Figure 4A,E) and cleaved caspase-3 (p=0.042; Figure 4C,E) as compared to lesions arising in vemurafenib-treated patients (n = 16; Figure 4B,D,E).
evidence: This is quantified by immunohistochemistry analysis of patient tumor samples.

claim: Significant apoptosis of epidermal keratinocytes was found in irradiated mouse skin that was suppressed by PLX4720 treatment (12.7 ± 0.4 apoptotic cells/mm vs 4.9 ± 0.3 apoptotic cells/mm skin, p<10−5).
source: Consistent with our other results, we found significant apoptosis of epidermal keratinocytes in irradiated mouse skin that was suppressed by PLX4720 treatment (12.7 ± 0.4 apoptotic cells/mm vs 4.9 ± 0.3 apoptotic cells/mm skin, [n = 3 pairs], p<10−5; Figure 4F,G), a finding corroborated by cleaved caspase-3 levels, which were induced within 6 hr of irradiation and suppressed in PLX4720-treated mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is quantified by histological counting of apoptotic cells in mouse epidermis.

claim: Phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 were significantly upregulated following UV irradiation and phospho-JNK was significantly suppressed by PLX4720 in mouse epidermis.
source: As expected, phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 were significantly upregulated following UV irradiation and phospho-JNK was significantly suppressed by PLX4720 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of mouse epidermal lysates.

claim: The upstream kinases MKK4 and MKK7 were activated by UV radiation and suppressed by PLX4720 at 1 and 6 hr post-irradiation in mouse epidermis.
source: The upstream kinases MKK4 and MKK7 were likewise activated by UV radiation and suppressed by PLX4720 at 1 and 6 hr post-irradiation, confirming the importance of this mechanism of PLX4720-induced JNK signaling suppression in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing phospho-MKK4 and phospho-MKK7 in mouse epidermis.

claim: Noxa mRNA expression was strongly induced by UV exposure, a response significantly dampened by PLX4720 treatment in mouse epidermis.
source: Finally, Noxa mRNA expression, as measured by qPCR, was strongly induced by UV exposure, a response significantly dampened by PLX4720 treatment (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is quantified by qRT-PCR analysis of Noxa mRNA levels in mouse epidermis.

claim: Within 20 days of administration of PLX4720, hyperkeratotic papules were visible on the backs of PLX4720-treated Hairless mice, which steadily grew into cSCC over the following several weeks.
source: Within 20 days of administration of drug, hyperkeratotic papules were visible on the backs of PLX4720-treated animals (Figure 5A,B), which steadily grew into cSCC over the following several weeks (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is documented by photographic and histological evidence of tumor development in drug-treated mice.

claim: Within 150 days (78 days of drug treatment), control-treated Hairless mice had not yet developed any visible lesions.
source: Within this period of 150 days (78 days of drug treatment), control-treated mice had not yet developed any visible lesions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown by tumor count data over time in control versus PLX4720-treated mice.

claim: Tumors from PLX4720-treated Hairless mice showed significantly lower levels of phospho-JNK (p=0.046) as compared to control-treated animals.
source: When we quantified the effects of each of these drug treatments, we found significant decreases in both phospho-JNK expression (p=0.046; Figure 5F,G,J) and cleaved caspase 3 expression (p=0.019; Figure 5H–J) in PLX4720-treated mice as compared to control-treated mice.
evidence: This is quantified by immunohistochemistry analysis of mouse tumors.

claim: Tumors from PLX4720-treated Hairless mice showed significantly lower levels of cleaved caspase 3 (p=0.019) as compared to control-treated animals.
source: When we quantified the effects of each of these drug treatments, we found significant decreases in both phospho-JNK expression (p=0.046; Figure 5F,G,J) and cleaved caspase 3 expression (p=0.019; Figure 5H–J) in PLX4720-treated mice as compared to control-treated mice.
evidence: This is quantified by immunohistochemistry analysis of mouse tumors.

claim: No mutations in Hras, Kras, or Nras were detected in any of the papillomas or carcinomas isolated from PLX4720-treated Hairless mice.
source: Importantly, we sequenced the entire coding regions for Ras (Hras, Kras, Nras) and found no mutations in any of the tumors in PLX4720-treated mice, as compared to one of 14 papillomas and carcinomas in a cohort of control-treated chronically-irradiated Hairless mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Sanger sequencing of RAS genes in mouse tumors.

claim: Both WT and Craf-deficient MEFs exhibited a significant colony formation advantage in the presence of PLX4720.
source: Both WT and Craf-deficient MEFs exhibited a significant colony formation advantage in the presence of drug (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar colony formation assays comparing drug-treated to control cells.

claim: The effect of paradoxical ERK activation is estimated to be 60% and other effects, including inhibition of JNK activity, account for 40% of the total colony growth advantage in MEFs.
source: Based upon this analysis, we estimated that the effect of paradoxical ERK activation to be 60% and other effects, including inhibition of JNK activity, to account for the rest (40%) of the total colony growth advantage (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is calculated from the difference in colony formation between WT and Craf-deficient MEFs treated with PLX4720.

claim: Untreated TKD HaCaT cells produced more colonies than SCR HaCaT cells suggesting that JNK pathway suppression results in an advantage in the absence of drug and paradoxical ERK activation.
source: Yet, untreated TKD HaCaT cells produced more colonies than SCR HaCaT cells suggesting that JNK pathway suppression results in an advantage in the absence of drug and paradoxical ERK activation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays comparing triple knockdown to control HaCaT cells without drug treatment.

claim: The effect of JNK pathway inhibition is estimated to be 17.6% based on HaCaT cell experiments.
source: Based on this, we estimated the effect of JNK pathway inhibition to be 17.6% (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is calculated from the colony formation advantage of TKD cells over control cells.

claim: JNK inhibition contributes approximately 17.6–40% of the total effect of PLX4720-accelerated colony formation.
source: When combined with the MEF experiment, we estimate that the effect of JNK inhibition contributes approximately 17.6–40% of the total effect of PLX4720-accelerated colony formation (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the quantitative estimates from both the MEF and HaCaT experiments.

claim: Clinical trial data on dabrafenib alone at 150 mg PO BID shows an overall aggregated cSCC rate of 6.1%.
source: However, clinical trial data on dabrafenib alone at 150 mg PO BID, shows an overall aggregated cSCC rate of 6.1% (Falchook et al., 2012; Hauschild et al., 2012; Long et al., 2012) vs 22% for vemurafenib at 960 mg PO BID in several hundred patients (Flaherty et al., 2010; Chapman et al., 2011; Sosman et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published clinical trial data.

claim: Vemurafenib at 960 mg PO BID has a cSCC rate of 22% in several hundred patients.
source: However, clinical trial data on dabrafenib alone at 150 mg PO BID, shows an overall aggregated cSCC rate of 6.1% (Falchook et al., 2012; Hauschild et al., 2012; Long et al., 2012) vs 22% for vemurafenib at 960 mg PO BID in several hundred patients (Flaherty et al., 2010; Chapman et al., 2011; Sosman et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published clinical trial data.

claim: Dabrafenib has little effect on apoptosis and JNK signaling at doses that are biologically equivalent to vemurafenib based upon growth inhibition of BRAFV600E melanoma cells and human pharmacokinetic data.
source: In stark contrast to vemurafenib, dabrafenib has little effect on apoptosis and JNK signaling at doses that are biologically equivalent based upon growth inhibition of BRAFV600E melanoma cells and human pharmacokinetic data (Falchook et al., 2012; Gowrishankar et al., 2012) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS and Western blot analysis comparing dabrafenib to PLX4720 at bioequivalent doses.

claim: Peak serum concentrations of dabrafenib at 150 mg PO BID in humans are over 50-fold lower (1.55 μM) than mean sustained serum levels of vemurafenib (86 μM) at 960 mg PO BID.
source: Peak serum concentrations of dabrafenib at 150 mg PO BID in humans (Falchook et al., 2012) are over 50-fold lower (1.55 μM) than mean sustained serum levels of vemurafenib (86 μM) at 960 mg PO BID (Flaherty et al., 2010), and the GI50 for the A375 melanoma cell line is less than 0.01 μM for dabrafenib (Greger et al., 2012) vs 0.50 μM for PLX4720 (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published pharmacokinetic data.

claim: At 0.05 μM, dabrafenib did not significantly impact UV-induced phospho-JNK upregulation or apoptosis in HaCaT and SRB1 cells.
source: Even at 0.05 μM, dabrafenib did not significantly impact UV-induced phospho-JNK upregulation or apoptosis in HaCaT and SRB1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and FACS analysis showing no effect of dabrafenib on JNK or apoptosis.

claim: ZAK is a significant off-target kinase for dabrafenib, but at 0.01 μM, over 64% of activity is retained.
source: We profiled dabrafenib activity against ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5, and found that ZAK is a significant off-target kinase for dabrafenib as well, but at 0.01 μM, over 64% of activity is retained (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays showing partial inhibition of ZAK by dabrafenib.

claim: Neither MKK4 nor MAP4K5 is substantially inhibited by dabrafenib up to 1 μM.
source: Neither MKK4 nor MAP4K5 is substantially inhibited by dabrafenib up to 1 μM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays showing no significant inhibition.

claim: Dabrafenib enhanced colony formation in WT MEFs, but not in Craf-deficient MEFs.
source: Using transformed WT and Craf-deficient MEFs in soft agar assays, we also showed that dabrafenib enhanced colony formation in WT MEFs, but not in Craf-deficient MEFs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar colony formation assays comparing dabrafenib effects in WT versus Craf-deficient cells.

claim: While both dabrafenib and vemurafenib cause equivalent paradoxical ERK activation in BRAF-wild-type cells, only vemurafenib confers a significant colony formation advantage in Craf-deficient cells that have no significant paradoxical MEK/ERK activation.
source: Our results suggest that while both dabrafenib and vemurafenib cause equivalent paradoxical ERK activation in BRAF-wild-type cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), only vemurafenib confers a significant colony formation advantage in Craf-deficient cells that have no significant paradoxical MEK/ERK activation, implicating off-target effects as a key difference between the two drugs with respect to cSCC development (Menzies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the effects of both drugs in Craf-deficient cells where paradoxical ERK activation is absent.

claim: RAS mutations are significantly enriched in cSCC arising in patients treated with vemurafenib relative to sporadic cSCC.
source: This is supported by the findings that RAS mutations are significantly enriched in cSCC arising in patients treated with vemurafenib relative to sporadic cSCC (Oberholzer et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012), and by the low rate of cSCC in patients treated with combined BRAFi and MEK inhibitor (MEKi) (Flaherty et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published studies on RAS mutations in vemurafenib-associated cSCC.

claim: The low rate of cSCC in patients treated with combined BRAFi and MEK inhibitor supports the role of paradoxical ERK activation.
source: This is supported by the findings that RAS mutations are significantly enriched in cSCC arising in patients treated with vemurafenib relative to sporadic cSCC (Oberholzer et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012), and by the low rate of cSCC in patients treated with combined BRAFi and MEK inhibitor (MEKi) (Flaherty et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from clinical trial data on combination therapy.

claim: The recently updated combination trial of the BRAFi dabrafenib and MEKi trametinib shows a low 7% cSCC rate in 54 patients.
source: The recently updated combination trial of the BRAFi dabrafenib and MEKi trametinib shows a low 7% cSCC rate in 54 patients, (Flaherty et al., 2012) suggesting that combined MEK inhibition can reduce, but not eliminate cSCC formation, nevertheless reinforcing a role for paradoxical ERK activation (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published clinical trial data.

claim: Combined MEK inhibition can reduce, but not eliminate cSCC formation.
source: The recently updated combination trial of the BRAFi dabrafenib and MEKi trametinib shows a low 7% cSCC rate in 54 patients, (Flaherty et al., 2012) suggesting that combined MEK inhibition can reduce, but not eliminate cSCC formation, nevertheless reinforcing a role for paradoxical ERK activation (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the clinical trial data showing reduced but non-zero cSCC rates with combination therapy.

claim: Many BRAFi-induced cSCC arise in sun-damaged skin.
source: The fact that many arise in sun-damaged skin suggests that prior chronic UV exposure is an important predisposing event (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published observations on the location of BRAFi-induced cSCC.

claim: Prior chronic UV exposure is an important predisposing event for BRAFi-induced cSCC.
source: The fact that many arise in sun-damaged skin suggests that prior chronic UV exposure is an important predisposing event (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cSCC arise in sun-damaged areas.

claim: Up to 30–40% of cSCC arising in vemurafenib-treated patients do not have RAS mutations.
source: While there is enrichment for RAS mutations in human cSCC arising in vemurafenib-treated patients vs controls (Oberholzer et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012), up to 30–40% of these lesions do not have RAS mutations.
evidence: This is cited from published mutation analysis of vemurafenib-associated cSCC.

claim: The Hairless mouse model has a very low frequency of Ras mutation in papillomas and carcinomas, more similar to sporadic human cSCC.
source: Unlike the DMBA/TPA model, in which lesions almost universally harbor Hras mutations (Brown et al., 1990), the Hairless model has a very low frequency of Ras mutation in papillomas and carcinomas (van Kranen et al., 1995), more similar to sporadic human cSCC.
evidence: This is cited from published characterization of the Hairless mouse model.

claim: p38 and JNK stress-activated MAP kinases are well-established critical mediators of UV-induced apoptosis.
source: Because the p38 and JNK stress-activated MAP kinases are well-established critical mediators of UV-induced apoptosis (Derijard et al., 1994; Chen et al., 1996; Tournier et al., 2000; Hildesheim et al., 2004), we explored the status of JNK and p38 activation by assessing phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 levels by Western blot (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is cited from established literature on UV-induced apoptosis mechanisms.

claim: BIM is upregulated by inhibition of ERK signaling.
source: This pro-apoptotic BCL2 family member is upregulated by inhibition of ERK signaling (Collins et al., 2005) and in BRAFV600E melanoma cells treated with vemurafenib (Paraiso et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published studies on BIM regulation.

claim: NOXA is a downstream effector of UV-induced apoptosis.
source: Since NOXA is a downstream effector of UV-induced apoptosis (Naik et al., 2007), we examined its expression and found that NOXA expression is induced by UV irradiation and suppressed by PLX4720 in all cell lines (Figure 1G), suggesting that inhibition of NOXA expression may be a mechanism of PLX4720-induced suppression of apoptosis.
evidence: This is cited from published literature on NOXA function in apoptosis.

claim: MCL1 is downregulated by UV exposure.
source: Finally, we examined the expression of the antiapoptotic BCL2 family member MCL1 because it is downregulated by UV exposure (Figure 1G), but as previously reported (Paraiso et al., 2011), unaffected by PLX4720 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing MCL1 levels decrease with UV but not with PLX4720.

claim: MCL1 is unaffected by PLX4720.
source: Finally, we examined the expression of the antiapoptotic BCL2 family member MCL1 because it is downregulated by UV exposure (Figure 1G), but as previously reported (Paraiso et al., 2011), unaffected by PLX4720 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and cited from previous literature.

claim: Signaling to JNK and p38 is intact in BRAFV600E melanoma cells.
source: Phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 were significantly upregulated following UV-irradiation (Figure 1H), showing that signaling to JNK and p38 is intact in BRAFV600E melanoma cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing induction of phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 in melanoma cells after UV.

claim: MKK4 and MKK7 are the two proximal kinases that synergistically phosphorylate JNK and are required for JNK activation.
source: Because JNK and p38 isoforms are not significantly inhibited by PLX4720 or vemurafenib directly, (Tsai et al., 2008; Bollag et al., 2010) we probed the phosphorylation status of MKK4 and MKK7 (MAP2K7), the two proximal kinases that synergistically phosphorylate JNK and that are required for JNK activation (Tournier et al., 2001; Haeusgen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from established literature on JNK activation mechanisms.

claim: JNK and p38 isoforms are not significantly inhibited by PLX4720 or vemurafenib directly.
source: Because JNK and p38 isoforms are not significantly inhibited by PLX4720 or vemurafenib directly, (Tsai et al., 2008; Bollag et al., 2010) we probed the phosphorylation status of MKK4 and MKK7 (MAP2K7), the two proximal kinases that synergistically phosphorylate JNK and that are required for JNK activation (Tournier et al., 2001; Haeusgen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published kinase profiling studies.

claim: Reported biochemical IC50s for vemurafenib and PLX4720 against multiple kinases including BRAFV600E, MAP4K5, SRMS, and BRK were quantitatively similar to the estimated Kd.
source: Reported biochemical IC50s for vemurafenib (Bollag et al., 2010) and PLX4720 (Tsai et al., 2008) against multiple kinases including BRAFV600E, MAP4K5, SRMS, and BRK were quantitatively similar to the estimated Kd, confirming the validity of this assay (Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing published IC50 values to the binding assay results.

claim: Single knockdown of MKK4 and MAP4K5 only partially suppresses UV-induced apoptosis or phospho-JNK induction in HaCaT cells.
source: Furthermore, single knockdown of MKK4 and MAP4K5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), only partially suppresses UV-induced apoptosis or phospho-JNK induction in HaCaT cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FACS and Western blot analysis of cells with individual kinase knockdowns.

claim: ZAK signals to both JNK and p38, but is principally necessary for activating JNK in stress-induced apoptosis.
source: These results are consistent with the model (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) that ZAK signals to both JNK and p38, but is principally necessary for activating JNK in stress-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of JNK and p38 suppression observed with ZAK knockdown and drug treatment.

claim: Off-target kinases in the JNK pathway are affected by vemurafenib/PLX4720 in all cells regardless of BRAF status.
source: Because off-target kinases in the JNK pathway are affected by vemurafenib/PLX4720, one expects that these kinases would be affected in all cells regardless of BRAF status.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the mechanism of off-target kinase inhibition.

claim: In BRAFV600E-expressing melanoma cells, the effect of blocking BRAF activity alone clearly dominates, because these cells are exquisitely dependent upon BRAF activity.
source: However, in BRAFV600E-expressing melanoma cells, the effect of blocking BRAF activity alone clearly dominates, because these cells are exquisitely dependent upon BRAF activity (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the known oncogene addiction of BRAFV600E melanoma cells and cited literature.

claim: The role of JNK in cancer is highly context-dependent and is partly related to differing functions of the individual isoforms and partial redundancy.
source: Our findings suggest a tumor suppressive role for JNK signaling in the context of drug-induced cSCC, though the role of JNK in cancer is highly context-dependent and is partly related to differing functions of the individual isoforms and partial redundancy (Tournier et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from literature on JNK function in cancer.

claim: Genetically-engineered mice lacking Jnk1 and Jnk2 have increased and decreased susceptibility, respectively, to chemical carcinogenesis in skin.
source: Genetically-engineered mice lacking Jnk1 and Jnk2 have increased (She et al., 2002) and decreased (Chen et al., 2001) susceptibility, respectively, to chemical carcinogenesis in skin, though these mice also have opposite defects in epidermal differentiation (Weston et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published mouse genetic studies.

claim: In mouse models, lack of Jnk1/2 activity suppresses Ras-driven tumorigenesis in lung.
source: In mouse models, lack of Jnk1/2 activity suppresses Ras-driven tumorigenesis in lung (Cellurale et al., 2011) and promotes it in Ras-driven and Trp53-deficient breast cancer models (Cellurale et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published mouse cancer models.

claim: In the context of Pten-deficiency, loss of Jnk1/2 or Mkk4/Mkk7 promotes aggressive prostate adenocarcinoma.
source: In the context of Pten-deficiency, loss of Jnk1/2 or Mkk4/Mkk7 promotes aggressive prostate adenocarcinoma (Hubner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published mouse prostate cancer models.

claim: JNK activity supports a pro-tumorigenic inflammatory microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Importantly, the effects of JNK on cancer are not always tumor cell autonomous, as JNK activity supports a pro-tumorigenic inflammatory microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published studies on JNK in liver cancer.

claim: Off-target inhibition of kinases, even at higher IC50s, can contribute biologically significant effects, particularly if they are in the same pathway.
source: We have shown that off-target inhibition of kinases, even at higher IC50s, can contribute biologically significant effects, particularly if they are in the same pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cumulative effects of inhibiting ZAK, MKK4, and MAP4K5.

claim: Kinase inhibitors must be considered in terms of their entire spectrum of activity, which can dramatically affect pathways distinct from those affected by inhibition of the intended target.
source: Finally, our results show that kinase inhibitors must be considered in terms of their entire spectrum of activity, which can dramatically affect pathways distinct from those affected by inhibition of the intended target.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the discovery of off-target effects on JNK signaling.
